title: A Tenth of a Second to Judge a Face
text:
In 2006 Janine Willis and Alexander Todorov of Princeton University measured how quickly people form first impressions from faces. They showed participants photographs of unfamiliar faces for just 100 milliseconds, half a second, or a full second, and asked them to judge each face on one trait, such as attractiveness, likability, trustworthiness, competence or aggressiveness.

The researchers compared these quick judgments with ratings that other people had made of the same faces with no time limit. Even after a tenth of a second, judgments already agreed strongly with the unhurried ratings. Trustworthiness was judged most consistently of all at the shortest exposure. Giving people more time did not change their judgments much. It mostly made them more confident, and allowed their ratings to become a little more differentiated.

The study did not show that these snap impressions are accurate. It measured only whether people agree with each other, and many judgments of character based on faces turn out to be wrong. What it showed is how fast and automatic such impressions are: by the time we have consciously looked at a stranger, we have already decided whether they seem trustworthy.
lesson: Your impression of a stranger forms in an instant and feels more certain than it is. Treat first impressions as guesses to test, not verdicts.
source: Willis, J., and Todorov, A. (2006). First impressions: Making up your mind after a 100-ms exposure to a face. Psychological Science, 17(7), 592-598.
